props.title: Don't Look Now
props.initialSlug: Grieving parents face supernatural horror in Venice

sections.content: Don't Look Now (1973) revolutionized psychological horror through Nicolas Roeg's masterful direction and fragmented editing style. Set in a haunting, wintertime Venice, the film follows grieving parents John and Laura Baxter (Donald Sutherland and Julie Christie) after their daughter's drowning death. Roeg's innovative use of premonitions, red motifs, and disorienting time jumps influenced decades of horror cinema, from The Shining (1980) to Hereditary (2018). The film's infamous love scene, with its intimate crosscutting between sex and aftermath, broke new ground in how cinema could portray both passion and dread simultaneously.

sections.content: Roeg's manipulation of time and reality created a template for supernatural thrillers that prioritize atmosphere over jump scares. Films like In the Bedroom (2001) and The Sixth Sense (1999) borrowed his technique of embedding crucial plot clues in seemingly mundane scenes. The director's background as a cinematographer shows in every frame - Venice becomes a maze-like character itself, its winding canals and decaying architecture reflecting the protagonists' psychological deterioration.

The film's influence on modern horror can't be overstated. Midsommar (2019) directly references Don't Look Now's color symbolism and grief themes, while The Others (2001) echoes its approach to parental trauma. The famous red coat motif has been copied countless times, most notably in Schindler's List (1993), showing how Roeg's visual language transcended genre boundaries. sections.content: Don't Look Now stands at the intersection of supernatural and psychological horror, creating a template for films that blur this distinction. Jacob's Ladder (1990) and Mulholland Drive (2001) followed its lead in presenting reality as fundamentally unreliable. The film's approach to grief and loss influenced a whole subgenre of "elevated horror" including The Babadook (2014) and A Ghost Story (2017), where supernatural elements serve as metaphors for psychological trauma.
